content.p: Guglielmo Libri was a celebrated mathematician, a friend of ministers and a member of the Académie des sciences in Paris. He was also, in the judgment of a French court in June 1850, a thief. As a government inspector of France's public libraries he is said to have carried off manuscripts and printed books on a scale that book dealers still cite when they talk about the history of book theft. He was sentenced in his absence to ten years in prison, never served a day of it, and died a free man in Italy in 1869. The full extent of his crimes was established only afterwards, by Léopold Delisle, a Bibliothèque nationale administrator, who reconstructed the thefts.
He is Guglielmo in Italian sources, and in France he was often called Guillaume.

Libri was born in Florence to a family of old Tuscan nobility; the Italian national biographical dictionary gives the date as 2 January 1802, while The Guardian says 1 January 1803. He entered the University of Pisa at 14, took his doctorate in 1820 and published his first paper on number theory the same year. In 1823 he was called to teach mathematical physics at Pisa, but within a year he had asked to be released from teaching so that he could visit the main scientific centres abroad.

Paris made his career. He befriended François Guizot, a historian who would later become France's Minister of Public Instruction, and he took part in the July Revolution of 1830. Back in Florence in 1831 he helped plan an uprising meant to force the grand duke to sign a constitution. The plot failed, police ordered him out of Florence, and he went back to Paris. There he became a French citizen in February 1833 and was elected to the Académie des sciences the following month, in the place left by the death of the mathematician Legendre. With the backing of the astronomer François Arago he began teaching at the Collège de France and, in 1834, at the Sorbonne.

His scholarship was real. His four-volume history of mathematical sciences in Italy, published between 1838 and 1841, is described by Treccani as a classic of the field, though only four of the six planned volumes appeared. He wrote for the Revue des deux mondes and sat on the editorial committee of the Journal des savants. He also made enemies. Treccani reports that quarrels over science and the running of the Académie earned him the hostility of Arago, and that the young mathematician Joseph Liouville pointed out errors in his papers. MacTutor adds that Liouville announced his well-known work on Évariste Galois in 1843 in answer to an attack by Libri.

Libri collected books obsessively. By 1841 he reckoned his own library held 1,800 manuscripts, and in 1847 he put his printed books at 40,000 volumes. Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania, who catalogued a bound set of pamphlets about his case, note that he also made a name as a critic of how libraries lost books, left them unattended and bought stolen ones.

French provincial libraries were, as the Penn account describes them, in disarray: since the Revolution they had been stuffed with books seized from clergy and aristocrats, and their staff were overwhelmed. Libri proposed to Guizot that a commission should survey and catalogue the manuscript holdings of public libraries across France. The Penn account says he became secretary of the commission, and an inspector, by 1842; Treccani dates the commission's creation to the summer of 1841. The job gave him long stays in provincial reading rooms, unsupervised time with collections, and he asked librarians to let him work after hours and send manuscripts to his home. According to the Penn account, many librarians were charmed by him and ignored the signs: the hours he spent with Italian scientific books when he was supposed to be cataloguing manuscripts, a visit to a back room where uncatalogued duplicates were kept, items that vanished after he had been through. Guinness World Records, which names him as the closest rival of the American Stephen Blumberg for the title of history's most prolific book thief, says his focus appears to have been manuscripts and handwritten items such as letters rather than printed books.

He was borrowing from libraries even before his official post. In 1836 he wrote to the Paris Observatory asking to borrow volumes of the astronomer Hevelius's correspondence and the letters of missionaries. The Bureau des longitudes recorded the loan in its minutes on 16 November 1836 and authorised a colleague to hand the volumes over. In his letter of request he promised to keep them only as long as strictly necessary.

Earlier still, Treccani records, his time as head of the library of Florence's Georgofili Academy ended in December 1826 with his resignation after a number of volumes had gone missing. He gave the academy an explanation that Treccani calls not very convincing, and the academy chose to avoid a scandal and drop the matter.

The Penn account lists what Libri did to hide the origin of what he took, according to what was later found. He is said to have reworked his recollections and receipts of genuine purchases so that illegally acquired items were folded in among them. He removed library stamps and other marks of ownership, had books rebound and restored so that they looked like different copies, and sent some to Italy to be bound in an Italian style that disguised where they had come from. He forged inscriptions to raise values, had restorers add blank leaves so that books could be sold as perfect copies, and added or altered title pages either to raise a book's value or to confuse its identity.

Suspicion fell on him from 1846. Anonymous letters about thefts reached the authorities. According to Treccani, after the first of them Libri put his valuable manuscript collection up for sale, and Lord Ashburnham bought it. Further anonymous denunciations led the royal prosecutor to open an inquiry, but Treccani says the file, which it calls short of solid proof, was shelved by Guizot. The Bureau des longitudes' account names the prosecutor as Félix Boucly and says that Libri, defending himself from London, claimed to have picked up many of the Paris observatory's volumes cheaply at a hurried sale of the effects of the astronomer Michel Lefrançois de Lalande. The judges were not persuaded, that account says, and built a case against him by checking library inventories for traces of his visits.

Guizot's protection ended with the February 1848 revolution and the proclamation of a new republic. Treccani says the dossier was published in Le National, the newspaper of Arago, who was by then a minister in the provisional government, and that Libri left hurriedly for England, where friends including A. Panizzi of the British Museum and the mathematician A. De Morgan supported him. The Penn account says he was tipped off, burned incriminating papers in the fireplace of his Paris apartment, sent 18 crates of books to London and hid the remaining papers and books. The Guardian puts the cargo at around 30,000 books and manuscripts packed in 18 big trunks, among them writings of Galileo and Copernicus. Guinness World Records cautions that Libri himself estimated his library at about 30,000 volumes in 1851 and that much of that was probably bought legitimately and the numbers likely inflated.

Legal proceedings against him were formally opened in March 1848 and a commission of inquiry was set up. The formal indictment, the Acte d'accusation, was published in May 1850 despite pamphlets in which Libri portrayed himself as a political persecutee and stressed what he said was a complete lack of proof. The trial opened in June, and the court sentenced him in his absence to ten years' imprisonment. Treccani remarks that the indictment was better argued than the original file, yet left room for doubt about the regularity of the investigation. He was struck off the rolls of the Légion d'honneur, the university, the Collège de France and the Académie des sciences.

Libri had defenders. The Bureau des longitudes' account mentions the writer Prosper Mérimée among them, and the archivist Ludovic Lalanne answered Mérimée in the Revue des deux mondes in May 1852 with a catalogue of what had been taken from the institutions concerned. The Penn set of pamphlets includes the work of a supporter who wrote under the name Bibliophile Jacob. In 1857, Treccani says, Libri managed to recover papers and some 15 thousand volumes of unsuspect origin still held in Paris, but a petition to the imperial senate asking for his rehabilitation was refused.

In London Libri carried on dealing. Treccani says he held ten auctions between 1849 and 1865 and wrote the catalogues himself, enriching them with historical notes on authors and printers, a style that made them useful to historians as well as collectors. The sources are generous about this side of him. Writing about his sales of 1861, a bibliographer quoted by MacTutor concedes that the unenviable reputation of a forger and thief should not blind anyone to the originality of the catalogues, and says Libri was among the first to steer English buyers toward scientific classics. A reviewer quoted on the same page nonetheless summed him up as a man with one misfortune: he was essentially a thief.

The Penn account notes that a 1859 Sotheby and Wilkinson sale described him as obliged to leave London for his health, though he did not in fact leave until about a decade later. His wife Mélanie died in 1865. He married the young English woman Helen de la Motte, in 1867, and in 1868 the couple went back to Italy to see relatives and friends who had kept their regard for him. He died at Fiesole on 28 September 1869 and was buried at San Miniato.

Treccani states that Libri's criminal responsibility was conclusively shown only after his death, through the meticulous work of Léopold Delisle, administrator of the Bibliothèque nationale, who reconstructed the thefts and forgeries. The Penn account dates the proof to 1883 and says that Delisle proved that 166 of the pieces Libri had sold to Lord Ashburnham in one big 1846 transaction were originally French national library property. The two accounts give different pictures of the Ashburnham sale: Penn places it in 1846, while Treccani says only that it followed the first anonymous accusation.

The recovery was slow and partial. In December 1871 the Bibliothèque nationale made available to the Paris Observatory volumes it attributed to Libri's diversions, including three folio volumes of Hevelius's observations, a bundle of 88 autograph letters torn from volumes of Hevelius's correspondence and 17 further items of letters and papers; the Bureau des longitudes recorded the handover in its minutes of 6 and 13 December. After Libri's death, according to The Guardian, the French government requested some manuscripts back and offered to purchase those already sold; a share came home, but tens of thousands of stolen items simply disappeared.

Treccani says Delisle brought the stolen manuscripts back to France in 1888 by negotiating their purchase from Ashburnham's heir, and that the rest of the Libri collection held by the Ashburnham family was bought by the Italian state in 1884 and deposited in Florence at the Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana. Lord Ashburnham, the Bureau des longitudes notes, was one of Libri's principal English buyers and knew nothing of the provenance of what he bought.

Pieces of the hoard still turn up. In June 2010 Haverford College in Pennsylvania returned to France a letter from René Descartes to Marin Mersenne, dated 27 May 1641 and concerning the publication of the Meditations. The Guardian reports that it was one of 72 Descartes letters Libri is said to have taken; it had sat in the college library since 1902 until a philosophy scholar at Utrecht University found a reference to it on the internet and the college offered to give it back. The Bureau des longitudes adds that stolen documents still appear in collections around the world and the Observatory buys back any that come up for sale.

An International League of Antiquarian Booksellers piece on theft and provenance cites him as an early case of book theft: an Italian count who used his position as Chief Inspector of French Libraries to take around 30,000 rare books and manuscripts, which later paid for a comfortable life in London society. The piece goes on to say that dealers' first wish is for libraries to conduct regular inventory inspections and to report missing items immediately.
